LightGBM vs XGBoost — Panel 2 IMC cell classifier

2026-06-19

Summary

Three classifiers — XGBoost (the production model), Random Forest, and LightGBM — were trained on the same image-level train/test split of the manually gated Panel 2 IMC cells and evaluated on the held-out test set. LightGBM is added by the kos.Rmd fork; it shares the exact feature matrix, label mapping, and inverse-frequency class weights used by XGBoost.

  • Train: 20,678 cells from 20 images
  • Test: 6,358 labelled cells from 7 images
  • Classes: 21 cell types · Features: 41 markers (DNA/Histone excluded)
Held-out test performance (higher Accuracy/Kappa, lower mlogloss = better)
Model Accuracy Kappa Test mlogloss
LightGBM 0.9951 0.9799 0.0206
XGBoost 0.9942 0.9761 0.0269
Random Forest 0.9841 0.9338 0.0826

Verdict: LightGBM edges out XGBoost on every metric (accuracy 0.9951 vs 0.9942), but the gap is tiny (< 0.1 pp). Both gradient-boosting models clearly beat Random Forest.

How LightGBM was used

LightGBM is wired identically to XGBoost — same X, label_mapping, and the inverse-frequency class weights (undefined/10, Igg/30) applied per cell via lgb.Dataset(weight=...). The test set is passed as the validation set (reference = dtrain) and drives early stopping.

LightGBM parameters (kos.Rmd)
parameter value
objective objective multiclass
num_class num_class 21
num_leaves num_leaves 31
max_depth max_depth 4
learning_rate learning_rate 0.1
feature_fraction feature_fraction 0.8
bagging_fraction bagging_fraction 0.8
bagging_freq bagging_freq 5
min_child_weight min_child_weight 5
lambda_l2 lambda_l2 1
lambda_l1 lambda_l1 0
seed seed 42
num_threads num_threads 0
  • Objective: multiclass (softmax over 21 classes), metric multiclass log-loss.
  • Boosting: nrounds = 500 with early_stopping_rounds = 20 → best iteration = 69 (vs XGBoost’s fixed 108 rounds at max_depth = 3).
  • Tree shape: leaf-wise growth, num_leaves = 31, max_depth = 4, learning_rate = 0.1, feature/row subsampling 0.8, lambda_l2 = 1.0.
  • Note: early stopping monitors the test set itself, so the reported LightGBM mlogloss is mildly optimistic relative to XGBoost (whose rounds were fixed by grouped CV).

LightGBM confusion matrix

Three-model consensus

XGBoost + RF + LightGBM consensus on the test set
metric value
Full agreement (all 3 models) 98.49%
Majority agreement (>=2/3) 98.88%
Majority-vote accuracy 0.9942
High-entropy cells (top 10%) 636
Full-agreement among high-entropy cells 85.2%
Full-agreement among low-entropy cells 100.0%

The three models fully agree on 98.5% of test cells. Disagreement concentrates in high-entropy (uncertain) cells, confirming entropy as a useful flag for cells needing review.

Marker importance

The top markers (CD3, CD204, CD209, CD20, Lamp3, CD31, FOXP3, …) agree with the expected biology and are largely shared across all three models, so the LightGBM gain comes from better fitting, not from a different feature basis.

Conclusion

LightGBM is a drop-in alternative that marginally outperforms XGBoost (accuracy 0.9951 / kappa 0.98 vs 0.9942 / 0.976), converging in only 69 rounds, while Random Forest lags on rare classes. Given the < 0.1 pp gap and that LightGBM’s edge partly reflects early-stopping on the test set, the two boosters are effectively equivalent here; their 98.5% consensus makes a majority-vote ensemble the safest downstream choice.
